finding.claim: The /settings/email state-changing endpoint uses @login_optional instead of @login_required, so unauthenticated requests reach set_email with g.uid = None. This is a missing authentication/authorization check on a sensitive account operation. Unauthenticated callers can trigger the email change, which can enable account takeover via password reset if set_email handles a None uid loosely, for example by updating a row with a NULL user or by matching the wrong record. The endpoint also has no CSRF protection.
finding.source: Any unauthenticated remote HTTP client sending POST /settings/email with no session cookie.
finding.sink: set_email(g.uid, ...) at routes.py:37, which changes the account email, with g.uid == None.

trace.note: login_optional sets g.uid = session.get('uid'), which is None when there is no session, and does not abort
set_email(g.uid, ...) is called with the None uid and no further check

finding.guards_checked: Compared with /settings/password at routes.py:42, which correctly uses @login_required (aborts 401 at lines 11-12). There is no inline check of g.uid in change_email. There is no CSRF protection or re-authentication. set_email is a stub (routes.py:48), so the impact depends on the real implementation, but the missing guard is on the route itself.

verdict.guard_found: none (login_optional at routes.py:19-25 only sets g.uid and never aborts; no inline g.uid check, no CSRF/re-auth)
verdict.reason: routes.py:34-37 exposes POST /settings/email with @login_optional (routes.py:22 sets g.uid=None without aborting) and calls set_email(g.uid, ...) with no check, unlike /settings/password's @login_required (routes.py:11-12); the stub at routes.py:48 means the real impact depends on its implementation, but the missing auth guard is real.
